title: Martin's cloak (c. 316–397)
hook: a soldier cuts his cloak in half for a beggar and dreams of Christ wearing it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyril's lectures and the word mystagogy: first the night, then the words. Your line was after, the meaning. Which gesture did you stop and ask about? Day seven hundred thirty.

A winter so cold, Sulpicius says, that people were dying of it. A young soldier named Martin rides up to the gate of the city of Amiens. At the gate stands a man with no clothes at all, asking the people going in and out for help. They pass him. Martin has already given away what else he had. All that's left is the cloak on his back and the sword at his side. And he looks at the cloak, and then at the sword.
screen: `A WINTER GATE.` → `A MAN WITH NOTHING.` → `A CLOAK AND A SWORD.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Sulpicius Severus, who wrote a life of Martin and says he knew him. Here's what he tells. Martin draws his sword, cuts the cloak in two, gives one half to the man, and wraps himself in what's left. Notice the half. He doesn't hand over the whole thing and ride off a hero. He shares it, and goes on looking a little ridiculous. Sulpicius says some of the bystanders laughed at how he looked. Others were ashamed, because they had more to give and hadn't given it. Then the night. Martin is asleep, and in a dream he sees Christ, wearing the half of the cloak he gave away. He's told to look closely and recognize it. And he hears Christ say to the angels around him, more or less: Martin, who is still only a catechumen, clothed me with this. A catechumen: someone still preparing for baptism. Martin wasn't even baptized yet. Sulpicius ties the dream to words of Jesus in Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Martin, Sulpicius says, didn't grow proud over the dream. He took it as a push, and went to be baptized. So the story has two halves, like the cloak. A man at a gate. And Christ, in the dream, wearing the same piece of cloth. The Catholic Church remembers Martin as a saint, a soldier who later became a monk and a bishop. It started with half a cloak.
screen: `HALF THE CLOAK, CUT WITH A SWORD.` · `SOME LAUGHED, OTHERS WERE ASHAMED.` · `CHRIST WEARING THE HALF.` · `STILL ONLY A CATECHUMEN.` · then, large: `YOU DID IT TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a coat or a blanket. Settle, and breathe. Start with the cold, not the closet. Where near you is someone likely to be outside tonight? A bus stop, a doorway, the steps of a church. Let one place come clear. Then ask what warm thing of yours could reach it: a coat you no longer wear, a spare blanket, a scarf, or the price of one, by way of a shelter, a coat drive or a parish collection. Choose one, and decide when it goes. If you pray, you can remember that person by name, or by the place they stand. The bell holds the time.
Martin's cloak. Half a soldier's cloak, cut with his sword for a freezing man, and worn by Christ in Martin's dream. Today's word.
Your line: half a cloak. Today, give one warm thing away, a coat, a blanket, or the price of one. Half counts. Day seven hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Martin of Tours as a saint; in parts of Europe his feast is kept with lantern processions and shared food, and some parishes run coat and blanket drives as winter begins.

fork.setup: you're Martin at the city gate in winter. a man with no clothes asks for help. you have a cloak and a sword. what do you do?
options: ride on; others will help him.
cut the cloak in two and give him half.
give him the whole cloak and freeze.
fork.reveal: he cut it in half and kept the rest, looking odd enough that some people laughed. that night he saw Christ wearing the half.

original.note: Latin (from Greek): the soldier's cloak Sulpicius says Martin cut in two.

trapdoor: what you thought: a generous saint gives a beggar his coat.
what it means: he gave half and kept half, and the dream says the half was given to Christ himself.
what a scholar hears: Sulpicius Severus, Life of Martin 3, which has Christ call him still a catechumen and ties the scene to Matthew 25.

Life of Saint Martin 3 paraphrased: severe winter; gate of Amiens; a naked poor man; Martin had already given away his other garments; cuts the cloak with his sword; bystanders laughing, others regretting they had not given; the dream, Christ telling the angels 'Martin, still a catechumen, clothed me with this garment'; Martin not proud but hastening to baptism. Confirm.
'Sulpicius ... says he knew him': Sulpicius describes visiting Martin in the Life (ch. 25). Confirm.
Original game: Latin 'chlamys' — confirm this is the word Sulpicius uses for the cloak.
